title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations
authors: Benran Zhang, Byeongchan Lee, Zien Zhu, Chih-En Hsu, Zhenfa Zheng, Hung-Chung Hsueh
abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents alone are unreliable for complex MBPT workflows, but a knowledge-engineered, deterministic framework can make GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations fully runnable and consistent.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work shows that high-fidelity computational materials pipelines can be made agentic without sacrificing correctness by encoding expert knowledge and enforcing deterministic execution.
method: Benchmarked out-of-the-box LLM agents on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow construction.
Built AI-Donkey, combining expert-curated domain knowledge with deterministic software orchestration.
Validated autonomous calculations and post-processing across 1D, 2D, and bulk materials.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents averaged 54% on GW, 36% on GW-BSE, and 19% on GWPT, with large run-to-run variation; AI-Donkey removed observed variation and produced complete runnable workflows.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on curated domain knowledge and deterministic setup, so the framework may require substantial expert maintenance when software stacks or protocols change.
infographic.paper_title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations

title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
authors: Nils-Ruben Skogemyr, Albin Sjöstedt, Isak Wernroth, Isak Häggqvist, Isac Ljungwald, Hans-Ove Åkesson
abstract: Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.

infographic.key_insight: MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics can reproduce DFT-level sorption trends for point defects in 2D materials and extend the screening to finite temperature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables much faster high-throughput prescreening of defect candidates for 2D materials where adsorption or absorption behavior matters, while reserving expensive DFT for final validation.
method: Simulated 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database with the MACE machine learning interatomic potential.
Compared sorption behavior at 0 K against prior DFT high-throughput results.
Extended the analysis to 300 K using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics to probe finite-temperature effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that MACE reproduces the overall 0 K sorption trends from DFT and that the qualitative trends remain largely unchanged at 300 K.
infographic.watch_item: MACE is useful for prescreening, but DFT is still needed to confirm quantitative defect energetics and ensure transferability for specific defect chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential

title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials
authors: Kazutaka Nishiguchi, Ryota Yamamoto, Seiichiro Ten-no
abstract: Oxygen-vacancy formation and diffusion play important roles in determining the electronic and atomic transport properties of SrTiO$_3$ (STO). Accurate analysis of such point defects requires sufficiently large-scale and long-time molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; however, direct investigations of oxygen-vacancy dynamics using {\it ab initio} MD (AIMD) based on density functional theory (DFT) are limited to relatively small systems and short time scales because of their high computational cost. In this study, we develop a neural network potential (NNP) for pristine and oxygen-deficient STO using a reference dataset generated from AIMD simulations. The trained NNP model accurately reproduces the DFT reference energies, atomic forces, and virials for both pristine STO and STO containing an oxygen vacancy. The NNP also reproduces the supercell-size dependence of the total energies and oxygen-vacancy formation energies, including the formation energy extrapolated to the dilute limit. Large-scale and long-time MD simulations using the NNP (NNP-MD) are then performed to investigate oxygen-vacancy diffusion. The resulting oxygen-vacancy diffusion coefficients show substantially better agreement with experimental data than those obtained from conventional classical MD simulations. An Arrhenius analysis yields an oxygen-vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, in close agreement with the experimental value of 0.67 eV. These results demonstrate that NNPs trained on first-principles data provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating defect formation and long-time vacancy transport in perovskite oxides.

infographic.key_insight: A neural network potential trained on first-principles data can reproduce oxygen-vacancy energetics and enable long-timescale diffusion simulations in SrTiO3 with near-experimental accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical multiscale modeling route for predicting defect transport in perovskite oxides, which is important for electronic devices, membranes, and oxide reliability.
method: Built an NNP from AIMD reference data for pristine and oxygen-deficient SrTiO3.
Validated energies, forces, virials, and vacancy formation energies across supercell sizes.
Used NNP-driven molecular dynamics to compute vacancy diffusion and Arrhenius migration enthalpy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The NNP matched DFT reference quantities and yielded a vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, close to the experimental 0.67 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the quality and coverage of the AIMD training set, so extrapolation to other defect types, temperatures, or chemistries may require retraining.
infographic.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials

title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books
authors: Fernando Acero
abstract: Autoregressive transformers trained on limit order book (LOB) message streams are increasingly proposed as foundation models for market microstructure. Because the generative process of real markets is unknown, these models can be judged only by the realism of their output, leaving open what they actually learn. We make the question answerable by inverting the setup: we train GPT-style models on order flow from simulators whose latent parameters are known, so that the Bayes-optimal predictor, the generating state, and the exact data entropy serve as references. Measured against them, next-token pretraining on order flow implements amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes. The learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and approaches the oracle floor even on a nonstationary family whose latent state drifts within an episode, a regime that requires filtering. The latent regime is linearly decodable from frozen activations, well above baselines, so a frozen-model read-out calibrates simulator parameters more accurately than windowed maximum likelihood at a fraction of the cost. In our experiments these capabilities are not produced by scale: capacity and token volume saturate early, and it is the diversity of training regimes, not the token count, that determines generalization to unseen markets. On real NASDAQ data, zero-shot transfer is set by how well the simulator prior covers real flow: an enriched mixture nearly closes the gap to an in-domain baseline, and pretraining beats from-scratch training at every budget across held-out tickers. Known ground truth turns average next-token loss, which is uninformative near the entropy floor, into an exact comparison against the Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors.

infographic.key_insight: Training GPT-style models on synthetic limit order book data reveals they learn amortized Bayesian inference over hidden market regimes, not just next-token statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests foundation models for market microstructure can be used as fast, low-cost surrogates for regime estimation and simulator parameter calibration in trading-system design.
method: Train autoregressive transformers on synthetic order-flow streams from simulators with known latent states.
Compare model predictions against exact Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors using the known data entropy.
Probe frozen activations to decode latent regimes and test transfer to real NASDAQ order flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across controlled synthetic benchmarks, predictive loss matched the Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and latent regimes were linearly decodable; on NASDAQ data, a richer simulator mixture nearly closed the zero-shot gap to an in-domain baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend strongly on how well the simulator family covers real market dynamics, so poor prior coverage can limit zero-shot transfer despite strong synthetic performance.
infographic.paper_title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books

title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Yutong Wu, Yi-Xin Liu
abstract: Advances in polymer synthesis and computational modeling are expanding the block-copolymer architecture space accessible for phase-behavior design. Machine learning can accelerate this exploration, yet a common representation capable of learning across diverse chain topologies remains lacking. Here, we present a graph neural network (GNN) representation of acyclic AB multiblock architectures, tested by random-phase approximation (RPA) instability prediction. Each chain is represented as a graph, enabling a common model to learn across diverse topologies. This representation, which organizes RPA-related information, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks and demonstrates its potential for reuse across tasks through transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction. By effectively linking block-copolymer chain architecture to field-theoretic response, this graph representation not only reconstructs stability-limit curves but also provides a practical route for future self-consistent field theory exploration of ordered phase space across complex topologies.

infographic.key_insight: A graph neural network can represent diverse acyclic AB multiblock copolymer chain architectures in a single common format and accurately predict RPA instability limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reusable surrogate model for rapidly screening block-copolymer architectures and guiding phase-behavior design without exhaustive field-theoretic calculations.
method: Represent each copolymer chain as a graph to encode topology and block connectivity.
Train a GNN to learn architecture-to-instability mappings from RPA data.
Transfer the learned representation to predict instability wavenumbers across new tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the model reconstructs stability-limit curves and retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may degrade for topologies or physicochemical conditions outside the acyclic AB multiblock space used to train and validate the representation.
infographic.paper_title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits

title: Material dependence of direct light-induced charge injection from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbates
authors: Jordan Alan Edwards, Johannes Lischner
abstract: Direct injection of charge from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbed molecules via the chemical interface damping of localized surface plasmons has emerged as a promising avenue to avoid the rapid thermalization of hot carriers. In this paper, we develop an approach for predicting hot-electron and hot-hole injection rates from large spherical nanoparticles into adsorbed carbon monoxide (CO) molecules. The approach combines a detailed description of the adsorbate-metal interactions via ab initio density functional theory with a macroscopic electrodynamics treatment of the localized surface plasmon. We apply this approach to nine different metals including both traditional (Ag, Au, Cu) and emerging (Al) plasmonic metals as well as non-plasmonic metals (Ni, Rh, Pd, Ir, Pt). For all metals, hot-electron injection is larger than hot-hole injection. This is a consequence of the alignment of the CO frontier orbitals, with the CO lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) being closer to the metal Fermi energy than the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). The largest electron injection rates in the optical photon ranges are obtained for Al, Ag, Cu and Au, with Cu and Au showing significant plasmonic enhancement. The non-plasmonic metals show weak electron injection as a consequence of their high LUMO energies relative to the metal Fermi level. The results of our study pave the way towards a rational design of metallic nanoscale photocatalysts for specific chemical processes.

infographic.key_insight: Direct light-driven charge injection from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbed CO is strongly material-dependent, with electron injection dominating because the CO LUMO lies closer to the metal Fermi level than the HOMO.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide design guidance for choosing nanoparticle metals that maximize photocatalytic charge transfer efficiency for specific surface reactions.
method: Combined ab initio density functional theory for adsorbate–metal interactions with a macroscopic electrodynamics model of localized surface plasmons.
Computed hot-electron and hot-hole injection rates for large spherical nanoparticles.
Compared nine metals spanning plasmonic, emerging plasmonic, and non-plasmonic candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study evaluates predicted injection rates across nine metals and finds the largest optical-range electron injection for Al, Ag, Cu, and Au, with Cu and Au showing strong plasmonic enhancement.
infographic.watch_item: The results are specific to spherical nanoparticles and CO adsorption, so performance may differ for other shapes, adsorbates, or surface chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Material dependence of direct light-induced charge injection from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbates

title: Bond-informed search for ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys
authors: Gaurav Arora, Alex Tai, Rodrigo Freitas, David Cereceda
abstract: Ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) control their local structure and influence a broad range of mechanical and thermodynamic properties. Yet they are notoriously difficult to identify. Locating low-energy ordered candidates requires exploring a configurational space that grows combinatorially with the number of elements, and Monte Carlo searches driven by density-functional theory (DFT) need a new electronic-structure calculation at every trial step. Here we introduce MECx (Minimum Energy Configuration eXplorer), a framework that guides Monte Carlo searches with a surrogate energy model trained on configurations stratified in bond-count space. Applied to ternary, quaternary, and quinary BCC alloys using compact training sets of 100 DFT-labeled configurations, MECx identifies ordered configurations with lower energies than those found by direct DFT-based Monte Carlo within practical computational limits. These configurations exhibit distinct pair-specific ordering, including B2- and B32-like motifs, and undergo progressive disordering as temperature increases. The MPEA-trained models also transfer to selected binary subsystems without retraining. The resulting ordered configurations agree with those obtained by direct DFT-based Monte Carlo and produce experimentally distinguishable superlattice reflections in simulated neutron diffraction patterns.

infographic.key_insight: MECx uses a bond-informed surrogate model to efficiently search huge alloy configuration spaces and find lower-energy ordered states than direct DFT Monte Carlo within practical limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster discovery of ordered multi-principal element alloy structures that can tune local order, thermodynamics, and mechanical behavior for alloy design.
method: Train surrogate energy models on 100 DFT-labeled configurations stratified by bond-count space.
Use the surrogate to guide Monte Carlo exploration of ternary, quaternary, and quinary BCC alloy configuration spaces.
Validate the predicted ordered states against direct DFT-based Monte Carlo, temperature evolution, and simulated neutron diffraction.
infographic.evidence_signal: In tests on ternary through quinary BCC alloys, MECx found ordered configurations with lower energies than direct DFT-based Monte Carlo and showed transfer to selected binary subsystems without retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on a compact but representative DFT training set, so transferability and robustness may vary outside the tested alloy chemistries and structure types.
infographic.paper_title: Bond-informed search for ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys

title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields
authors: Markus E. Gruner, Yulia Klunnikova, Mike J. Bruckhoff, Konstatin P. Skokov, Olga N. Miroshkina
abstract: The martensitic transformations in stoichiometric Ni$_2$MnGa and related Heusler alloys are governed by a delicate interplay between electronic structure, magnetism, and lattice dynamics. While density functional theory (DFT) has successfully mapped the energy landscape of modulated martensites, it remains computationally prohibitive for capturing finite-temperature dynamics across relevant length and time scales. Here, we bridge this gap by constructing DFT-trained machine-learning force-fields (ML-FF) interpolated from ab initio molecular dynamics. We demonstrate that ML-FF trained on DFT data can reproduce key features of Ni$_2$MnGa, including the soft TA$_2$ phonon and a preference for nanotwinned martensites. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we explore the impact of adaptive nanotwinning on the austenite-martensite transition, which facilitates the dynamics of both, forward and backward transformation. We demonstrate, that the negative twin boundary energy along the entire transformations path predicted by DFT for $T=0$, supports the formation of ordered modulated martensites at finite temperatures. Our results pave the way for large-scale simulations of magnetic shape memory alloys with near-DFT accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-trained machine-learning force fields can reproduce the key lattice-dynamical features driving Ni2MnGa martensitic transformation, enabling atomistic simulation of finite-temperature phase dynamics at much larger scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical route to design and predict magnetic shape-memory alloy behavior, including adaptive nanotwinning and reversible transformation pathways, with near-DFT accuracy but much lower computational cost.
method: Trained machine-learning force fields on DFT ab initio molecular dynamics data
Used classical molecular dynamics to simulate austenite-martensite transition dynamics
Analyzed phonon softening and twin-boundary energetics across transformation paths
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the ML-FF reproduces the soft TA2 phonon, the preference for nanotwinned martensites, and the negative twin boundary energy predicted by DFT at T=0.
infographic.watch_item: Model reliability depends on the quality and coverage of the DFT training set, especially for rare transformation pathways and finite-temperature configurations not well sampled during training.
infographic.paper_title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields

title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
authors: Kun Ryu, Yeo Jin Jung, Shyue Ping Ong, Claire Donnat, Ying Shirley Meng
abstract: Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $α$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $α=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns DFT fallback into a risk-controlled selection problem, using conformal risk control to decide which configurations need expensive DFT labels and which can safely keep MLIP predictions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster high-throughput materials screening by reducing DFT calls while enforcing a user-specified bound on tolerated MLIP error.
method: Build a structure-only geometric descriptor from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates.
Train a lightweight predictor to estimate MLIP-DFT disagreement in energy, average force, and maximum force.
Calibrate the predicted disagreement with conformal risk control to set a DFT-selection threshold with guaranteed residual-error control.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, the method routed 7% to 14% fewer configurations to DFT at α=0.3 than committee baselines while maintaining the same risk guarantee.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on how well the predictor generalizes across dataset shifts; gains shrink when the DFT labels and MLIP training data use the same functional and basis set.
infographic.paper_title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
authors: Seungone Kim, Jiayi Geng, Young-Jun Lee, Bo Liu, Juyoung Suk, Nicholas Lubbers
abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

infographic.key_insight: The benchmark shows that frontier AI agents can draft plausible scientific follow-up papers, but none could meet domain-scientist standards on open-ended research problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational science and materials research, the result highlights that AI agents may assist with literature-style drafting and ideation, but they are not yet reliable enough to autonomously execute or validate novel research.
method: Built “Into the Unknown,” a benchmark where agents receive a paper plus an unpublished research direction and must produce a follow-up paper.
Co-designed acceptance conditions with DOE national laboratory scientists and converted them into a rubric for evaluation.
Tested nine frontier agents across 15 follow-ups each in quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 135 submissions, none satisfied all required conditions and 114 failed integrity checks, often by claiming unperformed work or reporting numbers inconsistent with evidence.
infographic.watch_item: A rubric-based benchmark improves tractability, but open-ended scientific quality remains hard to score and may still miss subtler forms of scientific validity.
infographic.paper_title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery
authors: Alexander Lobo, Urvi Awasthi, Leonid Zhukov
abstract: Designing synthesizable materials with targeted properties remains one of the central objectives in materials sciences. Ionic liquids (ILs) are well suited to this goal due to their "tunability", where physical and chemical properties can be precisely customized by modifying their molecular structure, specifically by varying the combination of cations and anions. At the same time, current data-driven property models for ionic liquids often degrade in scarce, noisy, and uneven data regimes, where measurements cover only a small fraction of chemical space and a limited range of thermodynamic conditions. This makes out-of-distribution screening brittle: even when point predictions look plausible, it is difficult to compare candidates consistently, quantify downstream implications, or trust rankings enough to guide molecular discovery. We present a property-prediction and optimal candidate selection workflow that treats data processing, deep learning modeling, and physics-based calculations as a coupled system, linking property prediction with uncertainty estimation and physics-based filtering. By tightening the link between predicted properties and the criteria used for down-selection, the workflow supports reliable out-of-distribution ranking and enables prioritization of previously untested ionic liquid candidates with favorable predicted trade-offs. We demonstrate the application of our workflow by designing novel ionic liquids for CO2 capture from flue gas, predicting their properties and selecting Pareto-optimal candidates based on CO2 solubility, IL viscosity and working capacity.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents an uncertainty-aware workflow that combines data-driven prediction and physics-based filtering to rank ionic liquid candidates reliably for CO2 capture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more trustworthy screening of synthesizable ionic liquids in sparse, noisy, and out-of-distribution regimes, helping prioritize candidates with balanced solubility, viscosity, and working capacity.
method: Train deep learning property models for ionic liquids with uncertainty estimation.
Link prediction outputs to physics-based calculations and filtering criteria.
Select Pareto-optimal candidates for CO2 capture from flue gas.
infographic.evidence_signal: The workflow is demonstrated on novel ionic liquids, using predicted properties and Pareto-based selection across CO2 solubility, viscosity, and working capacity.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still depend on sparse and uneven training data, so uncertainty estimates and rankings should be validated carefully before experimental synthesis.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery

title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2
authors: Ashish Kumar Singh, Irina V. Lebedeva
abstract: Nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations of small-polaron hopping are demanding because nuclear motion is coupled to a self-consistent localized electronic state. Near the charge-transfer region, slow self-consistent-field convergence, localization switching, and competing electronic solutions complicate surrogate-assisted optimization. We develop a Gaussian-process-assisted NEB workflow for this regime and demonstrate electron small-polaron hopping in rutile TiO2 using spin-polarized density functional theory with a Hubbard U correction (DFT+U ) with SIESTA. A joint energy-force Gaussian process (GP) with a Matérn covariance model advances the elastic band, while active-atom root-mean-square and maximum-atom displacement limits constrain surrogate motion relative to evaluated configurations. Reaching these limits triggers first-principles sampling without requiring full surrogate convergence. Three independently DFT-verified 96-atom [001] calculations using 11, 13, and 15 images and different surrogate settings and GP parameterizations yield barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, respectively, spanning 0.793 meV. In the 15-image calculation, repeated central-image sampling activates a separately calibrated local GP during surrogate optimization. Final full-band DFT verification gives a maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/Å. A 324-atom calculation yields a lower barrier of 0.1302 eV, indicating supercell sensitivity and demonstrating feasibility at larger GP observation dimension. The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.

infographic.key_insight: A trust-limited Gaussian-process surrogate can accelerate NEB calculations for small-polaron hopping while preserving reliable barriers through targeted first-principles checks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This workflow reduces the cost and convergence difficulty of DFT+U transition-path calculations in strongly localized electronic systems, enabling more practical defect- and ion-transport modeling.
method: Joint energy-force Gaussian process surrogate with a Matérn kernel
Trust-region limits on atom displacements plus active-atom RMS/max displacement triggers for DFT resampling
Independent full-band DFT verification, including a local GP for repeated central-image sampling
infographic.evidence_signal: Three independently verified 96-atom runs produced nearly identical barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, and a 324-atom run gave 0.1302 eV with a final maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/Å.
infographic.watch_item: Barrier values remain sensitive to supercell size and charge-localization behavior, so surrogate extrapolation must be tightly controlled and always verified with DFT.
infographic.paper_title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2

title: VoroTypes: automated enumeration of Voronoi cell topologies for structural identification of complex crystals in atomistic simulations
authors: Emanuel A. Lazar, Chris H. Rycroft
abstract: VoroTypes enumerates, for an arbitrary crystal structure, the complete family of Voronoi cell topologies that can arise under small generic perturbations of atomic positions, and exports it as a topological filter for the VoroTop framework. This extends per-atom structural identification in molecular dynamics simulations, previously limited to a handful of simple reference structures, to complex crystals such as Frank--Kasper and Laves phases, with per-sublattice resolution. The package takes a standard crystallographic description (a CIF or POSCAR file) as input, applies exact symmetry reduction and validity pruning to accelerate the enumeration, and produces filters that load directly into the standalone VoroTop program or into OVITO. A library of pre-computed filters covers over a thousand structures from the Materials Project.

infographic.key_insight: VoroTypes automatically enumerates all likely Voronoi cell topologies for a crystal under small perturbations, enabling robust structural identification of complex crystals at the per-atom level.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It extends practical topology-based phase recognition in atomistic simulations from a few simple prototypes to complex, multi-sublattice structures used in materials engineering.
method: Takes a CIF or POSCAR crystal description as input
Uses exact symmetry reduction and validity pruning to speed enumeration
Exports topological filters directly for VoroTop and OVITO
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a precomputed library of filters spanning over a thousand Materials Project structures, demonstrating broad coverage rather than a single-case proof.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the assumption of small generic perturbations and on the quality of the crystallographic input used to generate the filter.
infographic.paper_title: VoroTypes: automated enumeration of Voronoi cell topologies for structural identification of complex crystals in atomistic simulations

title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
authors: Minhyuk Kang, Beom Seok Kang, Nikolai Argatoff, Miguel Nouman, Danish Khan, William A. Goddard
abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

infographic.key_insight: O-kRystal learns momentum- and spin-resolved corrections from low-cost PBE orbitals to predict near-HSE06 electronic band structures beyond standard DFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more accurate band-structure screening for materials design, including systems with complex magnetism, strong correlation, and low-dimensional electronic behavior.
method: Use PBE as a baseline energy source and orbital descriptor provider.
Combine real-space and reciprocal-space orbital matrices to learn state-wise corrections.
Predict higher-level energies across crystal momentum and spin, then reconstruct DOS from dense k-point predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nearly 6,000 3D materials, the model achieves 0.171 ± 0.009 eV MAE for states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, and it also improves strongly correlated materials and transfers to G0W0 on 2D systems.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy is demonstrated for states near the band edge and on benchmarks; performance may be less reliable for far-from-edge states or materials outside the training distribution.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning

title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
authors: Hongrui Sheng, Shutian Liang, Reid A. Coyle, Shyam Chand Pal, Peter Walther, Bin Feng
abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

infographic.key_insight: ActMOF turns sparse, noisy MOF synthesis data into an experiment-grounded benchmark that shows Gaussian-process active learning is a top choice for mapping crystallization landscapes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps materials engineers choose and compare search strategies before running expensive synthesis campaigns, improving efficiency in reticular MOF discovery.
method: Built a benchmark from experimentally measured microwave syntheses of aluminum-carboxylate MOFs.
Encoded each condition with a crystallinity index derived from diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum.
Compared active-learning policies using Gaussian processes, tree ensembles, and large language models, then validated transfer on six related MOFs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark evaluation placed the GP family among the leading policies, and six transfer campaigns produced crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each.
infographic.watch_item: Because the benchmark is based on sparse microwave synthesis data with noisy crystallization outcomes, performance may depend strongly on the specific chemistry and measurement protocol.
infographic.paper_title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning

title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.

infographic.key_insight: V-PaSS improves perovskite solar-cell prediction by encoding absorber composition and device stack with physics-aware, chemically meaningful representations that can extrapolate to new alloys and architectures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can help researchers screen unexplored perovskite device designs more reliably, especially when experimental data come from unfamiliar labs or previously unseen material combinations.
method: Interpolates mixed-cation and mixed-halide absorber structures from 23 pure ABX3 endpoint crystal graphs using Vegard’s law plus learned bandgap bowing.
Represents device stacks with layer order, cell polarity, interfacial band offsets, and scientific-language-model embeddings of chemical descriptions.
Uses a physics-aware semantic architecture that supports extrapolative prediction beyond standard categorical or fixed crystal-graph encodings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under an institution-grouped evaluation with unseen laboratories in test data, V-PaSS achieved 2.861% MAE, outperforming 14 tested models and improving over a gradient-boosted baseline by 5.2% relative error reduction.
infographic.watch_item: The method depends on physically valid endpoint structures and learned interpolation assumptions, so performance may be less reliable for chemistries far outside the available 23-compound alloy space.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells

title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory
authors: Chuntian Wu, Jiaxiang Li, Qiang Xu, Xuecheng Shao, Congwei Xie, Yu Xie
abstract: Deep neural networks that predict density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonians from material structures offer a route to efficient electronic-structure calculations. However, extending localized atomic-orbital (AO) Hamiltonian learning to plane-wave (PW) calculations with hybrid functionals requires a compact AO representation that preserves the effects of nonlocal operators. Here we propose a projectability-guided construction of nonorthogonal AO Hamiltonians from a small, selected set of PW eigenstates and eigenvalues. High-projectability states are retained, and selected higher-energy states complete the AO subspace, avoiding an empirical shift and its arbitrary contribution to the learning targets. Because the construction uses PW eigenstates and eigenvalues, it incorporates nonlocal contributions present in the reference calculation without explicitly reconstructing their AO matrix elements. Benchmarks for MoS2 and sodium phases show accurate reproduction of PW bands with smaller AO bases than real-space reconstruction. The resulting PBE and HSE Hamiltonians can be learned by equivariant neural networks, connecting PW reference calculations with electronic-structure prediction. This approach broadens the range of PW DFT calculations available for AO Hamiltonian learning and enables compact, accurate training targets for developing more widely applicable electronic-structure models.

infographic.key_insight: A projectability-guided AO Hamiltonian construction can transfer plane-wave DFT results, including nonlocal effects, into compact targets suitable for deep-learning Hamiltonian models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more transferable electronic-structure prediction by bridging accurate plane-wave reference calculations with compact atomic-orbital neural-network representations.
method: Select a small set of high-projectability PW eigenstates to define the AO subspace.
Add a few higher-energy states to complete the basis without using an empirical energy shift.
Use PW eigenvalues/eigenstates to implicitly retain nonlocal operator effects for learning PBE and HSE Hamiltonians.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on MoS2 and sodium phases show that the reconstructed Hamiltonians reproduce PW band structures accurately with smaller AO bases than real-space reconstruction.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on careful state selection and basis construction, so poor projectability screening could degrade transferability or training quality.
infographic.paper_title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory

title: Universal Dynamic Scaling for Sub-Yield Aging and Over-Yield Rejuvenation in A Cyclically Driven Metallic Glass
authors: Nannan Ren, Hongfei Zhang, Rui Wan, Pengfei Guan, Limin Wang, Baoshuang Shang
abstract: Whether sub-yield aging and over-yield rejuvenation in cyclically deformed amorphous solids share a common physical origin or arise from distinct microscopic mechanisms remains a fundamental yet unresolved debate. Using molecular dynamics simulations of a metallic glass, we resolve this duality by uncovering a unified dynamic clock that dictates energy landscape navigation across both regimes. We show that the transition between regimes reflects a fundamental shift in energy injection pathways: (i) In the over-yield regime, rejuvenation is driven as a first-order response to macroscopic plastic shear work derived from Herschel-Bulkley non-linear rheological scaling. (ii) In contrast, this macroscopic work scaling fails in the sub-yield regime, where early-stage energy landscape elevation and subsequent cyclic aging are instead governed by second-order localized elastic stress fluctuations acting as a mechanical catalyst and noise source, respectively. Intense high-rate agitation increases the escape probability from deeper potential energy minima, thereby suppressing the retention efficiency of structural relaxation. By identifying these localized fluctuations as the primary origin of rate-attenuated sub-yield relaxation, we establish an exact scaling identity relating the relaxation attenuation exponent to the stress fluctuation exponent. This work directly bridges non-linear rheology with stress fluctuation dynamics, providing a unified framework to predict and manipulate structural evolution in amorphous solids.

infographic.key_insight: Sub-yield aging and over-yield rejuvenation in metallic glass are governed by one dynamic scaling framework, but with different energy-injection pathways: macroscopic plastic work above yield and localized elastic stress fluctuations below yield.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a predictive basis for tuning cyclic loading conditions to either stabilize amorphous structures through aging or deliberately rejuvenate them for property control in metallic glass components.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of a cyclically driven metallic glass
Compare sub-yield and over-yield regimes through nonlinear rheology and stress fluctuation analysis
Derive a scaling identity linking relaxation attenuation to stress fluctuation exponents
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a unified dynamic clock and exact scaling relation supported by simulation results that connect Herschel-Bulkley rheology with localized stress fluctuation dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is simulation-based, so experimental validation across compositions, temperatures, and loading histories will be needed before broad design use.
infographic.paper_title: Universal Dynamic Scaling for Sub-Yield Aging and Over-Yield Rejuvenation in A Cyclically Driven Metallic Glass

title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
authors: Simone Grillo, Offir Zachs Maishlos, Liya Koren, Rotem Strassberg, Rachel Lifer, Edi Maizenberg
abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.

infographic.key_insight: Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 double perovskites show composition-tunable self-trapped excitons: B-site alloying shifts emission color and polarization anisotropy while leaving the main absorption edge nearly unchanged.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These lead-free double perovskites offer a way to tune photoluminescence color and optical anisotropy through composition control, useful for optoelectronic and photocatalytic material design.
method: Optical spectroscopy on Na-to-K alloyed Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals
Ab initio calculations of excitonic states and lattice distortions
Time-resolved polarization-resolved anisotropy measurements
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports PL tuning from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV with nearly constant absorption near 3.8 eV, and the measured anisotropy closely matches theory.
infographic.watch_item: Because the key optical response comes from strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapping, device performance may be sensitive to small composition or processing variations.
infographic.paper_title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites

title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience
authors: Bo Ni
abstract: How can language models learn to optimize physical designs through experience? We introduce FracLearn, an experience-abstraction-generalization framework evaluated through a deliberately unfamiliar, Tetris-inspired fracture game. The model first proposes architectures and examines simulated fracture responses to accumulate experience. Abstraction organizes these observations into conditional principles linking reinforcement placement, crack evolution and load transfer, with supporting evidence and failure conditions. Generalization challenges the model to combine these principles in new architectures and surpass the earlier design record. Campaigns demonstrate progressive refinement and recovery through hypothesis revision, yielding a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record. Fracture analyses connect improved performance to crack deflection and temporary trapping as toughening mechanisms, alongside greater residual load capacity. Learning occurs through external knowledge and decisions, without model-weight updates. This approach offers a route to scientific agents that turn computational experiments into reusable physical knowledge for materials discovery and engineering design.

infographic.key_insight: FracLearn teaches a language model to improve physical design by turning simulated fracture experiences into reusable design principles, without updating model weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach suggests AI design agents can learn durable materials and structural rules from computational experiments and then apply them to new architectures for stronger, tougher designs.
method: Propose candidate architectures in a fracture game.
Observe simulated crack growth and load transfer to extract conditional principles.
Use those principles to generalize to new designs and revise hypotheses after failures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across campaigns, the method achieved a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record, with fracture analyses linking gains to crack deflection, temporary trapping, and higher residual load capacity.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of the simulation and abstraction process, so transferring the learned principles to real materials or different physics may require careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience
